title: House Bill Would Let Deportation Orders Expire After 10 Years and Open a Green Card Path
excerpt: The Protect Our Neighbors Act, introduced by four California Democrats, would put a 10-year expiry on final removal orders and let some longtime residents apply for permanent residence.
body:
• Four California Democrats introduced H.R. 11120, the Protect Our Neighbors Act, on November 19: final orders of removal would expire 10 years after they were issued, for people continuously present in the US and not convicted of a crime.
  • A separate section would let the attorney general or the homeland security secretary cancel a qualifying removal order and grant a green card, for a fee of up to $1,200 with a certified copy of the applicant's latest federal tax return.
  • The sponsors say about 1.19 million people live in the US under final removal orders. The bill was prompted in part by the deportation of Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old East Bay grandmother removed in 2025 after more than three decades in California.
  • This is a proposal, not law: nothing changes today, there is no application to file, and the bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee. Affected readers should track the bill on Congress.gov and not pay anyone who claims they can file under it.

A final order of removal currently has no expiry date: it can be enforced years or decades after it was issued. A House bill introduced on November 19 would change that. The Protect Our Neighbors Act, H.R. 11120, introduced by Representative Lateefah Simon of California with Representatives John Garamendi, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas, would make every final order of removal expire 10 years after issuance and open a route to a green card for some of the people living under old orders.

Who is affected — exactly

The bill concerns one specific group: noncitizens who have already received a final order of removal, exclusion or deportation and who remain in the United States. According to the sponsors' announcement, about 1.19 million people live under final removal orders, many of them with removal delayed or suspended for years through deferred action or other circumstances while they work, pay taxes and raise families. The bill does not apply to people without a removal order, to people outside the United States, or — under its criminal-history conditions — to people convicted of a crime.

What would change

Under the text released by Ms. Simon's office, the bill would add a new section to the Immigration and Nationality Act stating that each final order of removal "shall expire on the date that is 10 years after the date on which such order was issued," provided the person has been continuously present in the country and has not been convicted of a crime. Expiry would not be entirely automatic in effect: an immigration judge could renew an expired order, but only on the homeland security secretary's motion, and only if the government shows by clear and convincing evidence that there was significant cause for the delay in executing the order unrelated to administrative or funding delays, and that renewal is in the public interest based on new evidence. That renewal standard is the bill's most consequential detail — the government could not revive an old order simply because it lacked the resources to enforce it sooner.

Once an order has expired and has not been renewed, the person could petition US Citizenship and Immigration Services for any lawful status for which they are eligible, after 10 years of continuous US presence and if never convicted of a crime punishable by more than a year. An expired order could not be renewed while such a petition is pending.

The separate green card path

A second section goes further for a narrower group. It would let the attorney general or the homeland security secretary cancel a qualifying removal order and adjust the person's status to lawful permanent resident — a green card. To qualify, the order would have to rest only on specified immigration violations: being present without admission or parole, lacking valid entry documents, misrepresentation, being present in violation of law, or failing to keep nonimmigrant status. The person must not have been removed within 10 years of the order, must have been released under an order of supervision or other conditional release without absconding, and must not be inadmissible on criminal, security, health or several other grounds. Applicants would pay a single fee of no more than $1,200 and file a sworn, certified copy of their most recent federal income tax return. The grant is discretionary — the text says officials "may" grant it.

"No one should have to live in constant fear of being torn away from their family and community after spending years building a life in this country."

— Representative Lateefah Simon, the bill's lead sponsor

The case behind the bill

The sponsors tie the bill to Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old Sikh grandmother from the East Bay who had lived and worked in California for more than three decades. ICE detained Ms. Kaur on September 8, 2025, at a routine check-in in San Francisco, and she was deported to India later that month; ICE said at the time that an immigration judge had ordered her removed in 2005. Her family, quoted in the sponsors' announcement, said they remain "traumatized and horrified" by her treatment. Representative Lofgren, a senior Judiciary Committee member and former immigration lawyer, said the country needs "a sensible immigration policy for those who have resided peacefully for a long time in America."

What to do next

Nothing — yet. The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee, has three cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors, and a bill number was posted as H.R. 11120 on Congress.gov. It would have to pass both chambers and be signed before anyone could apply under it, and the full official text had not been posted on Congress.gov as of late last week; descriptions so far draw on the version Ms. Simon's office released. If you live under a final removal order, the correct action today is unchanged: keep attending any scheduled ICE check-ins, keep your address current, and consult an immigration attorney about your existing options. Do not pay any service that claims it can file an application under this bill — no such application exists.
